tips.title: Check the Ministry of External Affairs travel advisory for your destination before you book, and take a do-not-travel warning seriously
tips.cost: Free. Ten minutes on the ministry's site, and another look a few days before departure.
tips.inPlainWords: India's Ministry of External Affairs publishes a travel advisory for each country on mea.gov.in, and the Indian mission in that country may issue its own notice. There is no four-level rating system in Indian practice and no list fixed in law: an advisory is administrative guidance, and it changes with a conflict, an outbreak or a natural disaster. Read it before you book and again a few days before you fly. If it says not to travel, that is a warning about your safety, not a formality to be weighed against the ticket price.
tips.benefit: The advisory comes from the MEA, and from the embassy or consulate for the country you are in; it also carries the consular contacts that matter in an emergency (item 2). Registering on the MADAD portal (madad.gov.in) puts your details with the mission before anything goes wrong (item 2). No Indian law forbids you to travel to a country under an advisory, and no immigration officer will stop you on that ground: the decision, and the risk, are yours.
tips.sources: Ministry of External Affairs, travel advisories. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>; MADAD portal. <https://www.madad.gov.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Advisories are revised at irregular intervals, so this book does not reproduce any of them — read the current page yourself and look at the date at the top; an advisory that has not been touched for years is common. If a country is in open conflict the mission may be unable to help, evacuation may not be possible, and a travel policy may exclude a risk that was already known when you bought it (item 4). A cheap ticket to a country under a do-not-travel warning is not a bargain.

tips.title: Save the MEA MADAD portal and the Indian mission's consular number before you travel, and write down the address
tips.cost: No cost to register. A replacement passport or an emergency certificate has a fee.
tips.inPlainWords: The Ministry of External Affairs runs the MADAD portal for Indians abroad, and each Indian embassy or consulate publishes a consular emergency number. Save the number, the address and the email before you leave, and give a copy to a family member at home. A consulate can help with a lost passport, an arrest or a medical emergency; it cannot pay your bills or get you out of jail.
tips.benefit: The MEA's MADAD portal registers a grievance and routes it to the mission. The consular officer can issue an emergency certificate, contact the local police or hospital, and inform your family. The Indian Community Welfare Fund can help with a limited emergency. Registering your travel and keeping a copy of the passport and visa helps the mission find you.
tips.sources: Ministry of External Affairs, MADAD. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>; Consular, Passport and Visa Division. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>; Indian missions abroad. <https://www.mea.gov.in/indian-missions-abroad.htm>
tips.caveats: A consulate cannot override the local law or pay a fine. Keep a digital and a paper copy of the passport. In a conflict, follow the mission's evacuation instructions.

tips.title: Understanding what consular protection can and cannot do: it can visit you, but cannot bail you out, and you still have to pay the costs
tips.cost: No cost at all. It only takes a few minutes to clearly understand these boundaries.
tips.inPlainWords: If you’re arrested abroad, what consulates can do is verify your situation locally, demand fair and lawful treatment, visit you, and attend court hearings as observers. They cannot overturn a verdict or take you away. Any expenses such as food, lodging, transportation, or medical care paid in advance by others must ultimately be covered by you. Therefore, before traveling abroad, make sure you have sufficient funds and insurance — don’t assume the government will cover everything if something goes wrong.
tips.benefit: When you’re detained, consulates can take several concrete actions. They can check your situation with local authorities and insist on fair treatment under both local laws and any relevant bilateral treaties. Consulates may also attend court sessions as observers and safeguard your right to a fair trial. If you’re injured or affected by a disaster, they can urge local emergency assistance and help your family handle aftermath matters.
tips.sources: Ministry of External Affairs. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Consulates cannot pay fines or medical bills on your behalf, nor buy plane tickets or overturn court rulings. What they can provide is information on local lawyers, interpreters, medical providers, and funeral services, plus help contacting family and finding relief resources. Knowing these limits is valuable: it reminds you to prepare sufficient funds and insurance before traveling — don’t rely on the assumption that the state will handle everything if trouble arises.

tips.title: Purchase insurance covering overseas medical care and medical evacuation — don’t settle for just flight delay coverage.
tips.cost: A short‑term travel insurance policy covering overseas medical needs typically costs anywhere from a few dozen to a few hundred rupees.
tips.inPlainWords: Medical expenses incurred abroad must be paid out of pocket. Domestic medical insurance rarely covers such costs, and embassies or consulates will not advance the money either. What can truly devastate a family financially is not routine outpatient care, but hospitalization following a serious injury — and the cost of repatriating the patient via a private jet or medical escort. When buying travel insurance, focus on two key coverage limits: overseas medical expenses and emergency medical evacuation/repatriation.
tips.benefit: Without adequate coverage, overseas medical treatment, extended hospitalization after trauma, and the expense of flying a patient back home can easily exceed hundreds of thousands of rupees. Therefore, selecting a policy with sufficient limits for both overseas medical care and emergency evacuation is essential.
tips.sources: U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Travelers' Health: Travel Insurance: "Medical evacuation insurance covers emergency transportation from a remote area to a high-quality hospital, which could otherwise cost more than $100,000.". <https://wwwnc.cdc.gov/travel/page/insurance>; The rest is the author's experience and there is no direct literature; Ministry of External Affairs. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The figure of $100,000 represents a minimum estimate rather than a full cost range. No official or industry‑wide statistics on typical evacuation costs are currently available, so this book does not list a broader range. Before purchasing a policy, verify three points: first, whether your destination country is covered; second, whether high‑risk activities such as scuba diving, skiing, or motorcycle riding are excluded; and third, whether claims are paid directly to hospitals or require you to pay upfront and then seek reimbursement. This advice applies even when traveling to visa‑free countries.

tips.title: Treat a high-paying overseas job with no interview and no written contract as a scam — and check the recruiting agent's registration under the Emigration Act, 1983
tips.cost: Checking the registration costs nothing. The money at risk is the agent's fee, the air ticket and the first month's salary that is often demanded up front — which is exactly why the check comes before any payment.
tips.inPlainWords: A recruiting agent who finds you a job abroad must be registered with the Protector General of Emigrants under the Emigration Act, 1983, and for a number of countries and job categories the worker also needs emigration clearance, processed through the eMigrate system run by the Ministry of External Affairs. Ask for the registration number and verify it before you pay anything. India has no rule that imposes a fixed travel ban for taking such a job, but a fake visa or a false statement to an immigration officer is an offence, and a passport can be impounded under the Passports Act, 1967.
tips.benefit: The lawful route is a registered recruiting agent and, where it applies, a valid emigration clearance: both are recorded in eMigrate, and the MEA has repeatedly warned about unregistered agents sending workers abroad on visit or tourist visas. Workers recruited to Myanmar and Cambodia for online fraud work have been reported repeatedly, and the missions have issued advisories about it. The warning signs are a salary far above the market for the skill, no interview, no written contract, a cash processing fee with no receipt, an instruction to fly to a third country first, and an offer to keep your passport safe. If the agent cannot show a registration number, a contract and a visa in your own name, walk away.
tips.sources: Ministry of External Affairs, eMigrate. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>; Emigration Act, 1983. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; eMigrate portal. <https://emigrate.gov.in/>; MADAD portal. <https://www.madad.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Do not hand your passport to an agent, and do not fly on a tourist visa to take up a job — that alone makes the employment illegal. A genuine employer pays for the work visa. If a relative has already gone and has stopped answering, contact the Indian mission and file a grievance on MADAD (item 2); a police complaint in the district where the agent operates is the second step, with the receipt, the contract and the agent's details.

tips.title: Check the foreign-exchange cash limit before you travel: India's LRS and the RBI rules cap what you can carry
tips.cost: A bank charges a margin and a fee; a money changer's rate is usually worse. A declaration is free.
tips.inPlainWords: Under the RBI's Liberalised Remittance Scheme, a resident can remit up to USD 250,000 a financial year for permitted purposes. Cash and travellers' cheques are subject to separate limits, and a very large cash amount must be declared at customs. Do not carry a friend's money or split a transfer to avoid the limit. Use a bank or an authorised dealer.
tips.benefit: The RBI's LRS sets the annual remittance limit, and the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 governs the rules. A traveller must declare currency above the customs threshold. A bank or an authorised money changer gives a receipt. Splitting a transfer to stay under the limit can be a violation. The Customs Act, 1962 applies to cash at the border.
tips.sources: Reserve Bank of India, Liberalised Remittance Scheme. <https://www.rbi.org.in/>; Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs. <https://www.cbic.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The LRS limit and the cash limit change; check the RBI and the customs rules before you travel. A 'hawala' transfer is illegal and leaves no legal recourse.

tips.title: Take photos of your passport, visa, and ID card and store them in the cloud; if lost, report to police first and then apply for a travel document.
tips.cost: No cost involved. Simply take a few photos before you depart.
tips.inPlainWords: If your passport is lost, the embassy or consulate can issue a travel document allowing you to return home, provided you can prove your identity. Having clear photos of the passport data page, visa pages, and entry/exit records greatly speeds up the replacement process. You must also report the loss to local police to obtain a police report, which is required for border checks and insurance claims. Since phones are often lost together with passports, do not rely solely on storing photos on your phone.
tips.benefit: When a passport is lost, foreign embassies or consulates can issue a travel document for repatriation, but only after you verify your identity. The speed of this process depends heavily on whether you possess clear photos of the passport data page, visa pages, and entry/exit records. Additionally, obtaining a police report is mandatory for border checks and insurance claims in many countries. Keep the consular number and the mission's address with the copy of your passport, so that you can give them to the officer writing the police report (item 2).
tips.sources: Ministry of External Affairs. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Store the photos in two separate locations — for instance, upload one set to cloud storage and send another to a trusted family member. Also print a hard copy and keep it apart from the original documents. Photograph your bank cards and prescriptions as well. Since phones and passports are frequently lost together, relying only on phone storage is insufficient. Cloud services often require SMS verification, which becomes impossible if your phone is lost; test access from another device before travel to ensure you can retrieve the files. Photos of official documents are sensitive information; encrypted storage is safer, but if you forget the password, no one can access them, so the copy sent to family members remains essential.

tips.title: Before driving abroad, check whether the country accepts an Indian licence or needs an International Driving Permit
tips.cost: An IDP fee is modest. A local test or a conversion costs more.
tips.inPlainWords: An Indian driving licence is not accepted everywhere. Many countries accept it for a short visit, but some require an International Driving Permit issued by an Indian automobile association, or a local licence after a residence period. Check the destination's transport authority before you rent a car. An IDP is a translation, not a substitute for a valid Indian licence.
tips.benefit: The Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 and the Central Motor Vehicles Rules govern the Indian licence. An IDP is issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention by an authorised automobile association. The destination's rules decide whether an IDP, a local test or a conversion is required. A rental company may ask for the IDP and the passport. Driving without the correct licence can void the insurance.
tips.sources: Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. <https://morth.nic.in/>; Motor Vehicles Act, 1988. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of External Affairs. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: A 'universal licence' sold online is not an IDP. The rules differ for a tourist, a student and a resident. Check the embassy and the rental company.

tips.title: Before paying a visa, study-abroad or immigration agent, find out which licence it actually holds — India has no general registration scheme for these agencies
tips.cost: Free to ask. The fee you should never pay is a large advance in cash before the agency shows you a written scope of work and the refund terms.
tips.inPlainWords: India does not license visa consultants or study-abroad agents as a class. The one registration that exists is for recruiting agents for overseas jobs, under the Emigration Act, 1983, with the Protector General of Emigrants, and it can be checked in the eMigrate system. An agency promising a guaranteed visa or a hundred per cent success rate is claiming something nobody can deliver, because the decision belongs to the foreign government. Ask for the licence where one applies, the fee and the refund terms in writing, and a receipt for every document you hand over.
tips.benefit: Where a licence exists it is the Emigration Act registration for overseas recruitment, and the Ministry of External Affairs has warned about unregistered agents. For study abroad and visa filing there is no licence at all: the protection is the contract and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, which covers a deficient service and a misleading advertisement, and a complaint can go to the district consumer commission. A false document submitted in your name is your problem, not the agent's: an honest refusal is a refusal, but a fraud finding follows the applicant.
tips.sources: Emigration Act, 1983. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of External Affairs, eMigrate. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>; Consumer Protection Act, 2019. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; National Consumer Helpline. <https://consumerhelpline.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Ask what exactly the fee buys, and what happens to it if the visa is refused; most agents keep it unless the contract says otherwise. Never sign a blank form, and never let an agent submit a document you have not read. Keep the original of every certificate — an agent who wants to hold your degree certificate or passport for weeks is a risk. If an agency takes the money and disappears, a consumer complaint and a police complaint are the two routes, and the second needs the receipts.

tips.title: Never sign an invitation letter, a sponsorship or an address proof for someone you do not know — the signature is yours and so is the case
tips.cost: Not signing costs nothing. Signing falsely costs a criminal case, a lawyer and the years it takes.
tips.inPlainWords: An invitation or sponsorship letter you sign is a statement to a foreign government, and if it turns out to be false you are the person who made it. India has no separate invitation-letter offence with a fixed fine: the exposure is ordinary criminal liability — cheating and forgery under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 — and, where a passport or a government form is involved, the Passports Act, 1967. The penalty is decided by a court, not by a published table.
tips.benefit: A visa officer decides on the papers in front of him, and an invitation is treated as evidence. If the visitor overstays or works illegally, the sponsor is the first person the mission and the Indian authorities ask about, and the file with your signature is the exhibit. There is no lawful way to help a stranger with a letter you cannot vouch for: invite only someone you actually know, state the relationship truthfully, and keep a copy of everything you send.
tips.sources: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Passports Act, 1967. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Ministry of External Affairs, passport and visa services. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: The same rule as carrying a parcel for a stranger: once you sign, you own the contents. A government servant or a member of the armed forces may also face service rules for helping a relative emigrate, so check the conduct rules before signing anything. If a friend asks for a letter as a favour, ask to see the visa form and the person's passport first — a request that dodges those two questions is the answer.

tips.title: Before traveling abroad, send your itinerary, accommodation details, and travel companions’ information to a family member, and agree on how often you’ll stay in touch.
tips.cost: No cost at all. Simply send a message before you leave.
tips.inPlainWords: An Indian mission can give a family at home the local police contact and tell them what the local process is. Once a police report is filed, the consulate follows up to ensure timely action. Whether this support chain can be activated depends on whether someone back home knows exactly where the traveler is and when they’re supposed to make contact. Sharing flight numbers, hotel addresses, companions’ phone numbers, and agreed-upon check-in intervals with one trusted person is sufficient.
tips.benefit: The Ministry of External Affairs runs the MADAD portal for grievances from Indians abroad, and every mission publishes a consular contact; a relative in India can file the grievance when the traveller cannot. The mission can then approach the local police or the hospital and pass information back to the family. None of that starts until someone at home knows the itinerary and can describe the traveller.
tips.sources: Ministry of External Affairs. <https://www.mea.gov.in/>; Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India. <https://irdai.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Include just four key details: flight number, accommodation address, companions’ full names and phone numbers, and the agreed contact frequency. If traveling to areas with poor signal or high crime rates, also specify exactly how long one should wait without contact before alerting local authorities. This measure costs virtually nothing, yet it serves as the essential prerequisite for activating all subsequent assistance procedures.

tips.title: Check destination regulations before traveling abroad with prescription medication, carry doctor certificates in English, and keep supplies within personal limits
tips.cost: Free. Involves spending 15–30 minutes checking the official health/customs website of your destination country and asking your doctor for an English-language medical summary or prescription.
tips.inPlainWords: Common prescription and over-the-counter medicines (such as ADHD medication, psychiatric drugs, codeine cough syrup, or cold medicines containing pseudoephedrine) may be strictly regulated or classified as prohibited controlled substances in foreign countries. Bringing them without advance authorization can lead to seizure, deportation, or criminal detention. Always check the destination country's health authority, carry medications in original packaging with doctor's documentation, and limit quantities to 1–3 months of personal supply.
tips.benefit: International regulations on personal pharmaceutical imports vary drastically. For instance, Japan's Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare (MHLW) and Narcotics Control Department mandate that travelers carrying medications containing controlled substances (such as psychotropics or narcotics) for personal medical use must submit an advance application and obtain an official import certificate at least 14 days prior to travel. Medications containing over 10% ephedrine/pseudoephedrine or over 1% codeine face strict limits. Japanese law limits personal imports of standard prescription drugs to a maximum of 1 month's supply (and other non-prescription drugs to 2 months' supply) without prior special administrative authorization. Singapore's Health Sciences Authority (HSA) restricts travelers to a maximum of 3 months' supply of non-controlled medications, requiring advance HSA approval for controlled substances, warning that exceeding limits results in confiscation and legal enforcement.
tips.sources: Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare, Narcotics Control Department. Application Guidance: Carrying controlled substances for personal medical use. <https://www.ncd.mhlw.go.jp/en/application2.html>; Japan MHLW Narcotics Control Department (2024). Controlled Substances List (Dec 12, 2024 edition). <https://www.ncd.mhlw.go.jp/dl_data/keitai/cotrolled_substances_list20241212%20.pdf>; Japan Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare. Information for those who are bringing medicines for personal use into Japan. <https://www.mhlw.go.jp/stf/seisakunitsuite/bunya/kenkou_iryou/iyakuhin/kojinyunyu/topics/tp010401-1_00001.html>; Health Sciences Authority, Singapore. Bringing in personal medications. <https://www.hsa.gov.sg/travelling-with-medication-and-medical-devices/personal-medications/>
tips.caveats: Regulatory rules evolve and vary by destination. Before departing, check the official health or border agency website of your transit and destination countries, or the consular travel advisories issued by your embassy. Cross-check active pharmaceutical ingredients against the local prohibited list rather than commercial brand names. Always keep medicines in original pharmacy packaging with patient name matching the passport. Never carry prescription medication on behalf of acquaintances or strangers (see Chapter 8, Item 29). Take high-resolution photos of prescriptions and packaging to store in cloud storage (Chapter 21, Item 7).

tips.title: When you fly back to India, do not carry meat, dairy, fresh fruit, vegetables or seeds, and declare any animal or plant product on the Red Channel
tips.cost: Free. Skip the perishable food souvenir and check the bag before you check in. If you are unsure about an item, the Red Channel costs a few minutes and a form.
tips.inPlainWords: India restricts the entry of fresh fruit, vegetables, seeds, plants, meat and dairy, and the customs baggage rules require a passenger to declare what is being carried. Prohibited items are seized and destroyed, and an undeclared item can be confiscated with a penalty under the Customs Act, 1962. You do not have to guess: use the Red Channel and let the officer decide.
tips.benefit: The Plant Quarantine (Regulation of Import into India) Order, 2003, made under the Destructive Insects and Pests Act, 1914, lists what may not be imported without a permit and is enforced by the plant protection service at ports and airports. The Directorate General of Foreign Trade's import policy and the Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying control meat, dairy and live animals, and a pet dog or cat needs an import permit and a health certificate. A passenger's baggage is governed by the Customs Act, 1962 and the Baggage Rules made under it: undeclared goods can be confiscated and a penalty imposed, and the amount is assessed by the officer.
tips.sources: Plant Quarantine (Regulation of Import into India) Order, 2003. <https://ppqs.gov.in/>; Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs. <https://www.cbic.gov.in/>; Directorate General of Foreign Trade. <https://dgft.gov.in/>; Customs Act, 1962. <https://www.indiacode.nic.in/>; Department of Animal Husbandry and Dairying. <https://dahd.gov.in/>
tips.caveats: Do not pack food as a gift for a relative and assume it will pass: the rule looks at the item, not the intention. A sealed, commercially manufactured, shelf-stable product is treated differently from fresh produce, so declare it and let the officer decide. Keep the receipts for anything valuable. The same logic applies in the other direction — the destination country's rules apply when you land, not the Indian rules when you leave.
